lessons.title: Surds
lessons.objective: Simplify surds, rationalise denominators and compare surd expressions without a calculator.

content.heading: Surds
paragraphs: A candidate writes √50 − √18 = √32 and loses the mark. Surds only combine after each one is reduced to its simplest form.

content.heading: What a surd is and how to simplify
paragraphs: A surd is an irrational root left in root form, such as √2, √3 or √5. √4 is not a surd because it equals 2; the test is whether the root is rational.
Simplify by splitting the number into a perfect-square factor and a remainder: √12 = √(4 × 3) = 2√3, and √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2. Pull out the largest square you can see.
Only like surds combine. 3√5 + 2√5 = 5√5, but 3√5 + 2√3 stays as it is. Multiplication and division work inside the root: √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).
bullets: A surd is an irrational root.
Extract the largest perfect square.
Only like surds add or subtract.
content.takeaway: Reduce every surd before you add, subtract or compare.

check.question: Simplify √75.

content.heading: Rationalising the denominator
paragraphs: A fraction is not simplified while a surd sits in the denominator. Rationalising multiplies top and bottom by something that clears the root.

For a single surd, multiply by that surd: 1/√3 × √3/√3 = √3/3. For a binomial, multiply by the conjugate, which changes the sign between the terms: 1/(√5 + 1) × (√5 − 1)/(√5 − 1) = (√5 − 1)/(5 − 1) = (√5 − 1)/4.
The conjugate works because (√a + b)(√a − b) = a − b², a difference of squares that removes the root. Write the new denominator as a minus b², then simplify the fraction if a common factor remains.
bullets: A surd denominator must be cleared.
Single surd: multiply by itself.
Binomial: multiply by the conjugate.
content.takeaway: The conjugate turns a surd denominator into a difference of squares.

check.question: Rationalise 2/√2.
check.why: Multiply top and bottom by √2: 2√2/2 = √2.

visual.caption: Choose the multiplier from the shape of the denominator.

content.heading: Comparing and equating
paragraphs: To compare surds, square both sides and compare the squares. Since the surds here are positive, squaring preserves the order: 3√2 and 2√3 become 18 and 12, so 3√2 is larger.
To find coefficients in an expression such as (a + b√c)², expand and match the rational part and the surd part separately. The two parts cannot cancel each other.

Check by squaring back. If a simplification gives 2√2, then (2√2)² = 8, which should match the original quantity. A decimal estimate also catches gross errors: treating √2 as 1.414 is enough to rule out an option that is wildly wrong.
bullets: Compare surds by squaring.
Match rational and surd parts separately.
Square back to check.
content.takeaway: Squaring removes the root and makes comparison exact.

check.question: Which is larger, 2√5 or 3√2?
check.why: Squaring gives 20 and 18; since 20 is larger, 2√5 is larger.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Reduce every surd to its simplest form before answering. The options are usually written in lowest terms.

steps.reason: Only lowest-form surds reveal whether the terms can combine.
steps.predictPrompt: Both terms now carry √2. What happens next?

steps.reason: Like surds add and subtract exactly like like terms.
Squaring should return the value of the original expression.

lessons.title: Indices
lessons.objective: Apply the laws of indices to simplify expressions and solve exponential equations by matching bases.

content.heading: Indices
paragraphs: A candidate rewrites 4^x = 8 as 2^x = 3 and loses the mark. The bases must match before the indices can be compared.

content.heading: Laws that come from counting factors
paragraphs: An index counts how many times a base is multiplied by itself. Because a^m means m copies of a, multiplying a^m by a^n gives m+n copies, so a^m × a^n = a^(m+n).
Division cancels copies: a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n). A power of a power repeats the whole block n times, so (a^m)^n = a^(mn). The same counting gives (ab)^m = a^m b^m and (a/b)^m = a^m/b^m.
Any non-zero base to the power zero is 1, because a^m ÷ a^m = a^0 and also equals 1. Zero itself is excluded, since 0^0 is undefined.
bullets: Multiply powers of the same base by adding indices.
Raise a power to a power by multiplying indices.
Any non-zero base to the power zero equals 1.
content.takeaway: Every law is a shortcut for counting repeated factors.

check.question: Simplify 2^3 × 2^4.
check.why: The bases are the same, so add the indices: 3 + 4 = 7.

content.heading: Negative and fractional powers
paragraphs: A negative power is a reciprocal: a^-m = 1/a^m, so 3^-2 = 1/9. The minus sign does not make the value negative; it moves the power across the fraction line.
A fractional power is a root: a^(1/n) = the nth root of a, so 8^(1/3) = 2. A general fraction applies the root first and the power second: a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m, so 27^(2/3) = 3^2 = 9.
Take the root before the power when the numbers are large, because the root keeps them small. Convert every root to a fractional power before applying the laws.
bullets: A negative index means reciprocal.
A fractional index means root.
Root first, then raise to the power.
content.takeaway: A negative index flips the fraction; a fractional index takes a root.

check.question: Evaluate 16^(3/4).
check.why: The fourth root of 16 is 2, and 2 cubed is 8.

visual.caption: The operation on the indices changes with the structure of the expression.

content.heading: Equations and traps
paragraphs: To solve an exponential equation, write both sides with the same base and equate the indices. For 4^x = 8, rewrite as (2^2)^x = 2^3, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2.
If the terms are multiplied, add the indices first: 2^x × 2^(x+1) = 32 becomes 2^(2x+1) = 2^5, so x = 2. If the bases cannot be matched directly, factor each term into a common base.
Watch the traps. (a+b)^2 is not a^2+b^2, and a^m × b^n cannot be combined into one base. Also note that 2x^2 means 2(x^2), while (2x)^2 = 4x^2, and -2^2 = -4 while (-2)^2 = 4.
bullets: Match the base before equating indices.
Add indices before solving a product.
Respect brackets and signs.
content.takeaway: Most index equations are solved by the single move of matching bases.

check.question: If 9^x = 27, what is x?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Convert every expression to a single base before comparing powers. Most index questions test that one move.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations
lessons.objective: Solve ax² + bx + c = 0 by factorisation, the formula or completing the square, and use the sum and product of roots.

content.heading: Quadratic equations
paragraphs: A candidate factorises x² + 3x = 10 without moving the 10 and gets the wrong roots. Standard form comes first.

content.heading: Standard form and factorisation
paragraphs: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to zero. It has two roots, sometimes repeated. Rearrange before doing anything: x² + 3x = 10 becomes x² + 3x − 10 = 0.
To factorise with a = 1, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For x² + 3x − 10, the pair is 5 and −2, so (x + 5)(x − 2) = 0 and x = −5 or x = 2.
When a is not 1, split the middle term using a pair that multiplies to ac and adds to b, then group. A product is zero only when one factor is zero, which is why each bracket gives a root.
bullets: Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 first.
Find a pair that multiplies to c and adds to b.
Set each bracket to zero.
content.takeaway: A quadratic must be in standard form before it can be solved.

check.question: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0.
check.why: The pair −3 and −4 multiplies to 12 and adds to −7, so (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0.

content.heading: Formula and completing the square
paragraphs: When factorisation is not obvious, the quadratic formula always works: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. Substitute carefully, keeping the signs.
The discriminant b² − 4ac tells the nature of the roots: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots.
Completing the square rewrites x² + bx as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)². It is longer than the formula but gives the vertex of the curve, which matters when a question asks for a maximum or minimum.
bullets: The formula always works.
The discriminant predicts the roots.
Completing the square reveals the vertex.
content.takeaway: Use the formula for speed and completing the square for the vertex.

check.question: What is the discriminant of x² + 4x + 4 = 0?
check.why: b² − 4ac = 16 − 16 = 0, so the equation has one repeated real root.

visual.caption: Factorisation is faster when it works; the formula always works.

rows.left: The pair is easy to see

content.heading: Roots and word problems
paragraphs: For ax² + bx + c = 0, the sum of the roots is −b/a and the product is c/a. Check x² + 3x − 10 = 0: the roots 2 and −5 sum to −3 and multiply to −10.
To build an equation from its roots, use x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0. If the roots are 3 and 4, the equation is x² − 7x + 12 = 0.
Word problems are the same process in disguise. Translate the sentence, solve, then reject roots that cannot make sense, such as a negative length or age.
bullets: Sum of roots = −b/a.
Product of roots = c/a.
Reject impossible roots in word problems.
content.takeaway: The sum and product of roots check the answer and rebuild the equation.

check.question: For 3x² − 7x + 2 = 0, what are the sum and product of the roots?
check.why: Sum = −b/a = 7/3 and product = c/a = 2/3.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: After finding roots, check their sum and product against −b/a and c/a. It takes seconds and catches most sign errors.

lessons.title: Trigonometry
lessons.objective: Use the basic ratios, special angles, identities and the sine and cosine rules to solve triangles.

content.heading: Trigonometry
paragraphs: A candidate uses the sine rule on a triangle with two sides and the included angle and gets stuck. Choosing the right rule starts with naming what is known.

content.heading: Ratios and special angles
paragraphs: In a right-angled triangle, SOHCAHTOA gives sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Label the sides against the angle before choosing a ratio.
The special angles appear in almost every paper. sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2; cos runs the same values in reverse; tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1 and tan 60° = √3.
Use exact values rather than decimals when the options are in surd form. The identity tan θ = sin θ/cos θ links the three ratios and explains why tan 45° = 1.
bullets: SOHCAHTOA names the three ratios.
Learn the 30°, 45° and 60° values.
Prefer exact surd values to decimals.
content.takeaway: Label the sides first, then choose the ratio that connects them.

check.question: What is sin 60°?
check.why: The sine of 60° is √3/2; 1/2 is sin 30° and √2/2 is sin 45°.

visual.caption: Sine and cosine are the same ratios read from opposite sides.

content.heading: Identities and quadrants
paragraphs: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 holds for every angle. It lets you find one ratio from another: if sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, cos θ = 4/5.

Beyond 90°, the sign depends on the quadrant. ASTC — all, sin, tan, cos — records which ratios are positive in the first, second, third and fourth quadrants. A reference angle gives the size, and the quadrant gives the sign.
Useful reductions follow: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ, and tan(180° + θ) = tan θ. Sketch the angle to confirm the sign rather than memorising every case.
bullets: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle.
ASTC gives the sign by quadrant.
Use a reference angle for the size.
content.takeaway: The quadrant decides the sign; the reference angle decides the value.

check.question: What is sin 150°?
check.why: 150° is in the second quadrant, where sine is positive, and its reference angle is 30°, so sin 150° = 1/2.

content.heading: Non-right triangles
paragraphs: For triangles without a right angle, use the sine rule or the cosine rule. The sine rule is a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; use it when you know a side and its opposite angle.
The cosine rule is a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. The area formula is 1/2 ab sin C.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north as three-figure angles, such as 045° or 315°. Draw the north line at each point before applying either rule.
bullets: Sine rule: a side and its opposite angle.
Cosine rule: two sides and the included angle.
Bearings are clockwise from north.
content.takeaway: Choose the rule from the information given, not from habit.

check.question: Which rule should you use when you know two sides and the included angle?
check.why: The cosine rule uses two sides and the angle between them to find the third side.

visual.caption: The known information decides which rule can be used.

rows.right: Two sides and the included angle

rows.left: Pair each side with its opposite angle
rows.right: Use the included angle, not any angle

content.body: Check that your calculator is in degree mode, and settle the sign from the quadrant before you compute.

lessons.title: Probability
lessons.objective: Use sample spaces, complements and the and/or rules, including draws without replacement.

content.heading: Probability
paragraphs: A candidate draws two balls without replacement and keeps the original denominator for the second draw. The bag has changed, so the probability must change too.

content.heading: Sample space and complement
paragraphs: Probability compares favourable outcomes with all equally likely outcomes: P(A) = favourable/total. It always lies between 0 and 1, with 0 impossible and 1 certain.
The sample space is the set of all outcomes. Two coins give 4 outcomes, two dice give 36, and a coin with a die gives 12. Listing the space prevents double counting.

The complement rule is P(not A) = 1 − P(A). It is fastest for 'at least one': with three coins, P(no head) = (1/2)³ = 1/8, so P(at least one head) = 7/8. The phrase 'at least one' is the signal to use the complement rather than count every case.
bullets: P(A) = favourable / total.
Probability lies between 0 and 1.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
content.takeaway: List the sample space before you count anything.

check.question: If P(A) = 3/8, what is P(not A)?
check.why: The complement is 1 − 3/8 = 5/8.

content.heading: Union and intersection
paragraphs: 'Or' points to the union and 'and' to the intersection. For any two events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), because adding both counts the overlap twice.
If the events are mutually exclusive they cannot happen together, so P(A and B) = 0 and the rule becomes P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

If the events are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Dependence changes the second probability, which is why drawing without replacement needs adjustment. Independence is about influence, not about whether the events can happen together.
bullets: 'Or' adds, but subtract the overlap.
Mutually exclusive events have no overlap.
Independent events multiply.
content.takeaway: Decide whether the events can overlap or affect each other before choosing a rule.

check.question: P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3, with A and B independent. What is P(A and B)?
check.why: For independent events, multiply: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

visual.caption: Overlap and influence decide which probability rule applies.

rows.left: A coin shows head or tail

content.heading: Without replacement
paragraphs: Without replacement, the first draw changes the second. Both the favourable count and the total fall by one, so the second probability uses the new numbers.
For a bag with 3 red and 2 blue, P(both red) = (3/5)(2/4) = 6/20 = 3/10. With replacement, the bag resets and the second probability stays 3/5.

Multiply along a branch for 'and', and add across branches for 'or'. A tree diagram keeps the counts visible and prevents using the original denominator twice. Label each branch with the probability at that moment, not the starting probability.
bullets: Both counts fall by one without replacement.
Multiply along branches for 'and'.
Add across branches for 'or'.
content.takeaway: After a draw without replacement, redraw the bag before the next probability.

check.question: A box has 4 green and 6 yellow pens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(both green)?
check.why: The first draw is 4/10 and the second is 3/9, so the product is 12/90 = 2/15.

visual.caption: Replacement resets the bag; no replacement changes every later draw.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Write the sample space and the remaining counts before multiplying. Most probability errors are counting errors, not formula errors.

lessons.title: Number Bases
lessons.objective: Convert numbers between decimal and other bases and add numbers written in a different base.

content.heading: Number Bases
paragraphs: A shop in Jos prices a bag at 34 in base five. A candidate who reads it as thirty-four loses the mark. The base is the place value system, not the number itself.

content.heading: What a base is
paragraphs: A base is the number of symbols a system uses. In base ten the symbols are 0 to 9 and each place is ten times the one to its right. In base five the symbols are 0 to 4 and each place is five times the one to its right.
A digit must therefore be smaller than the base. The digit 5 cannot appear in base five because the system has only 0 to 4. That test alone rejects a distractor without any calculation.

The rightmost place is ones, the next is base, the next is base squared. A three-digit base-five number 243 is therefore 2×25 + 4×5 + 3 = 73 in decimal. The position, not the shape of the digit, decides the value.
bullets: In base b, each place is b times the one to its right
Digits must be smaller than the base
Place values are 1, b, b² and so on
content.takeaway: A digit must be smaller than the base, and place values are powers of it.

check.question: Which number cannot be written in base five?
check.why: 5 is not a base-five digit, so 354 cannot be a base-five number.

content.heading: Converting between bases
paragraphs: To convert from base b to decimal, expand by place value. In base three, 210 is 2×9 + 1×3 + 0 = 21. In base two, 1011 is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. The expansion is the method.

To convert from decimal to base b, divide repeatedly by b and read the remainders upward. To write 25 in base five: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 remainder 0, 5 ÷ 5 = 1 remainder 0, 1 ÷ 5 = 0 remainder 1, so 25 is 100 in base five. The remainders, read upward, are the digits.

To convert directly between two non-decimal bases, pass through decimal. A number in base three is first expanded to decimal and then divided into base five. A direct shortcut does not exist, which is why the pass is the method.
bullets: Base b to decimal: expand by powers of b
Decimal to base b: divide by b, read remainders upward
Between two non-decimal bases: pass through decimal
content.takeaway: Expand to decimal from any base, then divide to a new base.

check.question: What is 210 in base three in decimal?
check.why: 2×9 + 1×3 + 0 = 21, so 210 in base three is 21 in decimal.

content.heading: Adding and subtracting in another base
paragraphs: Addition in base b works like decimal addition except that the carrying threshold is b. In base five, 3 + 3 = 11 because 6 is one five and one unit. The carry is therefore smaller than in decimal.
Subtraction needs borrowing in the same way. In base four, 31 − 12 needs one four borrowed as four units. The method is identical to decimal, only the threshold and the borrow amount change.
Multiplication by a single digit also follows the threshold. In base five, 4 × 4 = 31 because 16 is three fives and one unit. A table of products up to base minus one is therefore enough.
bullets: Carry at b, not at ten
Borrow b units, not ten
Single-digit products use the same threshold
content.takeaway: Do the arithmetic in the base, carrying and borrowing at b.

check.question: What is 33 + 24 in base five?
check.why: 3 + 4 = 12 in base five, so the result is 122; 57 is the decimal sum, not the base-five sum.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any conversion, test the digits. A digit equal to or greater than the base cannot occur, so it rejects a distractor at once. Then expand or divide; never convert between two non-decimal bases directly.

steps.reason: Each digit must be smaller than four
steps.result: 1, 3 and 2 are valid, so 132 is a base-four number

steps.reason: Place values in base four are 16, 4 and 1

The last remainder is the most significant digit

content.heading: Go deeper: Why base ten is a habit, not a law
paragraphs: Base ten is used because humans have ten fingers. It is a habit of counting, not a property of numbers. A number written in base five is the same quantity as a number written in decimal, only the place values differ.

That is why a bag priced at 34 in base five is not thirty-four in the price. The digits are the same, but the place values are 25, 5 and 1 rather than 100, 10 and 1. The base must therefore be read before the number.
Examiners test that habit directly. A question that asks for a base-five sum in decimal is testing whether the candidate converts, not whether the candidate can add. The conversion is the skill.

That is why a bag priced at 34 in base five is not thirty-four in the price. The digits are the same, but the place values are 25, 5 and 1 rather than 100, 10 and 1.
Base ten is therefore a cultural fact rather than a mathematical law. That distinction is why a number in another base can be mistaken for a decimal one.

The same digits in different bases are different quantities
The base must be read before the number

content.heading: Go deeper: Base two and the computer
paragraphs: Base two uses only 0 and 1 because a circuit can be on or off. Each place is a power of two, so a byte of eight bits can represent 256 values. That economy is why computers count in binary.
A binary number such as 1011 is therefore 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. The expansion is the same as in any base, only the place values are powers of two. The method does not change with the base.
A hexadecimal digit therefore packs four binary digits. That packing is why one hexadecimal digit can stand for a whole byte, which is how addresses are written in fewer symbols.
A binary number such as 1011 is therefore 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. The expansion is the same as in any base, only the place values are powers of two.
The eight bits of a byte can therefore represent 256 values. That economy is why a byte is the unit of storage.
bullets: Base two uses 0 and 1 for on and off

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap in a base question
paragraphs: The trap is a digit that is valid in decimal but invalid in the base. A candidate who does not test the digits will add 5 in base five and get a sum that cannot be written. That test is therefore the first step.

The second trap is a decimal sum that looks like a base sum. In base five, 33 plus 24 is 122, while in decimal it is 57. A candidate who adds in decimal and writes 57 has answered a different question.
Time must be budgeted as in comprehension. A conversion that resists can be left and returned to. A test that is finished is worth more than a perfect answer to three items.
That budget is why a first sweep is useful. The easy conversions can be answered at once, and the hard ones can be left until the base is clear.
The trap is therefore the option that is correct in sense but wrong in form. A candidate who reads only for meaning will choose it.
bullets: Test the digits before any calculation
A decimal sum is not a base sum
Do an easy-first sweep and return to hard items

lessons.title: Modular Arithmetic
lessons.objective: Use remainders modulo a number to solve congruences and to test divisibility without long division.

content.heading: Modular Arithmetic
paragraphs: A trader shares 17 yams equally among 5 customers. One yam is left over. That remainder is a modular statement, not a division.

content.heading: Remainders and the meaning of modulo
paragraphs: For a positive integer m, the remainder of a on division by m is the number left after subtracting the largest multiple of m that fits. That remainder lies between 0 and m − 1. It is written a mod m.
Two numbers are congruent modulo m when they leave the same remainder. That is written a ≡ b (mod m) and means m divides a − b. In mod five, 17 ≡ 2 and 12 ≡ 2, so 17 ≡ 12.
A remainder is therefore a class, not a single number. All numbers congruent to 2 mod five form one class, which contains 2, 7, 12, 17 and so on. The class is the object of study.
bullets: a mod m is the remainder between 0 and m − 1
a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a − b
A congruence class is all numbers with that remainder
content.takeaway: Modulo keeps only the remainder, so numbers with the same remainder are congruent.

check.question: What is 38 mod 7?
check.why: 35 is the largest multiple of 7 below 38, so the remainder is 3.

content.heading: Arithmetic on remainders
paragraphs: Remainders add and multiply without leaving the modulus. To find (a + b) mod m, add a mod m and b mod m and reduce again. To find (a × b) mod m, multiply the remainders and reduce again.
Powers therefore reduce at each step. To find 7^3 mod 5, note 7 ≡ 2, so 7^3 ≡ 2^3 = 8 ≡ 3. Working with remainders instead of the whole numbers is why modular arithmetic is short.
Negatives reduce by adding the modulus. In mod five, −1 ≡ 4 and −3 ≡ 2. That reduction lets a subtraction be done as an addition, which is often shorter.
bullets: Add remainders, then reduce; multiply remainders, then reduce
Reduce powers at each step
Negatives reduce by adding the modulus
content.takeaway: Keep every intermediate as a remainder, not as a whole number.

check.question: What is 7×8 mod 5?
check.why: 7 ≡ 2 and 8 ≡ 3, so the product is 2×3 = 6 ≡ 1 mod 5.

content.heading: Solving congruences and divisibility
paragraphs: A linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m) is solved by undoing the multiplication. If a and m are coprime, a has an inverse modulo m, and x ≡ a⁻¹b (mod m). The inverse is the number that multiplies a to give 1.
Divisibility is a congruence to zero. A number is divisible by m exactly when it is congruent to 0 mod m. Testing divisibility is therefore testing a remainder, not performing a division.

A congruence system combines remainders. The Chinese remainder idea is that a number is determined by its remainders modulo pairwise coprime moduli. Those moduli therefore describe the number without naming it.
bullets: ax ≡ b (mod m) is undone by the inverse of a
Divisible by m means congruent to 0 mod m
Remainders modulo coprime moduli determine the number
content.takeaway: A congruence is a remainder statement, and an inverse undoes a multiplication.

check.question: Which number is divisible by 9?
check.why: The digit sum of 3,681 is 18, a multiple of 9, so it is congruent to 0 mod 9.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Reduce every number to its remainder before any operation, and reduce again after it. A product that is never reduced grows too fast to compute, while a product of remainders stays under the modulus throughout.

steps.reason: 13 ÷ 7 leaves 6, so 13 ≡ 6 mod 7
6^2 = 36 is small enough to reduce directly
steps.result: 36 mod 7 = 1, because 35 is a multiple of 7

content.heading: Go deeper: Why remainders are enough
paragraphs: A remainder is enough because only the remainder decides divisibility and congruence. Two numbers with the same remainder behave alike in every addition and multiplication, so the whole numbers can be replaced by their remainders.
That replacement is why a large power can be computed in a few steps. Instead of 13^2, the work is done on 6^2. The answer is the same because the remainders are congruent.
An examination rewards that shortness. A candidate who reduces early finishes in seconds, while one who multiplies out runs out of time. The remainder is therefore a time skill as well as a concept.

content.heading: Go deeper: Inverses and when they exist
paragraphs: An inverse of a modulo m is a number that multiplies a to give 1. It exists exactly when a and m are coprime, that is, when they share no common factor greater than one. That coprimality is therefore the condition.
The inverse can be found by trial because m is small in an examination. In mod five, the inverse of two is three because 2×3 = 6 ≡ 1. That trial is a valid method when m is small.
A linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m) is then solved by multiplying both sides by that inverse. If a and m are not coprime, there may be no solution or many, which is why the condition matters.

content.heading: Go deeper: Divisibility tests as congruences
paragraphs: A number is divisible by m exactly when it is congruent to 0 mod m. The familiar tests are congruences in disguise. The test for three and nine uses the digit sum because ten is congruent to one modulo three and nine.

The test for eleven uses alternating digits because ten is congruent to minus one modulo eleven. That alternation is therefore a congruence, not a trick. The test for four uses the last two digits because one hundred is divisible by four.
A candidate who understands those tests can derive them. A candidate who memorises them can only apply them. The derivation is therefore the deeper skill.
That derivation is why a new test can be invented in an examination. If a modulus is given, its test can be built from the value of ten modulo that modulus.

lessons.title: Fractions and Decimals
lessons.objective: Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and convert between fractions and decimals.

content.heading: Fractions and Decimals
paragraphs: A trader shares three oranges equally among five customers. Each customer gets three-fifths of an orange. That sharing is a fraction, and its decimal form is 0.6.

content.heading: What a fraction means
paragraphs: A fraction a/b means a divided by b. The top is the number of parts taken and the bottom is the number of parts in a whole. A fraction is therefore a division, not only a pair of numbers.

An improper fraction has a top greater than its bottom, as in 7/4. Its mixed form is 1 and 3/4, because one whole is four quarters. Conversion between the two forms is therefore a division with remainder.

A fraction can equal one when top and bottom are equal, be less than one when the top is smaller and be greater than one when the top is larger. That comparison decides the size before any calculation.
bullets: a/b means a divided by b
Improper fractions convert to mixed fractions by division
Top smaller than bottom means less than one
content.takeaway: A fraction is a division, so its size is read from top against bottom.

check.question: Which fraction is greater than one?
check.why: The top is greater than the bottom, so the fraction is greater than one.

content.heading: Adding and subtracting fractions
paragraphs: Fractions add by a common denominator. To add a/b and c/d, write both over bd and add the tops. The denominators therefore become the same before the tops are added.
The sum must then be reduced. A fraction that shares a common factor can be divided by that factor. Reduction is therefore the final step of every addition.
Subtraction follows the same rule with a minus in place of a plus. The common denominator is still the first step, and reduction is still the last.
bullets: Add over a common denominator, then reduce
Subtract over a common denominator, then reduce
Reduction follows every addition and subtraction
content.takeaway: Find a common denominator first, add or subtract the tops, then reduce.

check.question: What is 1/3 + 2/3?
check.why: The denominator is already common, so the tops add to 3 over 3, which is 1.

content.heading: Decimals and conversion
paragraphs: A decimal is a fraction whose denominator is a power of ten. Tenths are tenths, hundredths are hundredths and thousandths are thousandths. A terminating decimal therefore becomes a fraction over a power of ten.
A recurring decimal does not terminate. Its repetend is shown by a dot or a line, and it converts to a fraction by a short algebraic step. The repetend is therefore the mark of a recurring decimal.
Rounding a decimal to a stated place looks at the next digit. If that digit is five or more, the last kept digit rises by one. That rule decides the final digit.
bullets: Decimals are fractions over powers of ten
Recurring decimals convert by an algebraic step
Round by the next digit: five or more rises
content.takeaway: Decimals are fractions over powers of ten, and rounding looks at the next digit.

check.question: What is 0.75 as a fraction?
check.why: 0.75 is 75 hundredths, which reduces by 25 to 3/4.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any fraction operation, name the denominator first. If it is not common, make it common before touching the numerators, and reduce at the end. A fraction that is never reduced is marked as incomplete.

steps.reason: 3 and 4 multiply to 12, so 12 is common

hints: Multiply the denominators for a common one

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the common denominator works
paragraphs: A fraction counts parts of a whole. Two fractions can only be added when their parts are the same size, which is what a common denominator provides. That sameness is why the denominators must match.

Multiplying top and bottom by the same number does not change a fraction. That equivalence is why 2/3 and 8/12 are the same quantity. The common denominator is therefore not a trick, but a change of size.
Reduction then returns the fraction to its smallest parts. A fraction that is not reduced is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Examiners therefore mark the reduced form.
That reduction is why cancelling is valid. A common factor in top and bottom counts the same parts twice, so removing it simplifies the count.

content.heading: Go deeper: Multiplying and dividing fractions
paragraphs: Multiplication needs no common denominator. Multiply top by top and bottom by bottom. That direct method is why multiplication is shorter than addition.
Division by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal. To divide by 2/3, multiply by 3/2. That inversion is why a division question becomes a multiplication question.
Cancelling before multiplying saves work. If a top and a bottom share a factor, divide them first. A candidate who cancels early therefore keeps the numbers small.
That cancelling is the same reduction as in addition, only earlier. Examiners reward it because it prevents a large fraction that must then be reduced.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recurring decimals and approximations
paragraphs: A recurring decimal does not terminate because its denominator has a prime factor other than two or five. Its repetend therefore repeats forever. That repetition is why it converts to a fraction.
The conversion sets x equal to the decimal and uses the repetend to eliminate it. A decimal that starts with a non-repeating part needs a longer step. That step is algebraic, not arithmetic.
An approximation rounds a decimal to a stated place. That rounding must follow the next digit, not the size of the number. A candidate who rounds by guesswork therefore loses the mark.
That rule is why 0.75 rounds to 0.8 to one decimal place. The next digit is five, so the kept digit rises.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.objective: Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and solve profit, loss and simple interest problems.

content.heading: Percentages
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha keeps 15 out of every 100 customers. That share is 15 per cent. The denominator is always one hundred.

content.heading: What a percentage means
paragraphs: A percentage is a fraction over one hundred. Fifteen per cent is 15/100, which reduces to 3/20. That reduction is why a percentage can be a fraction without changing its value.

A decimal converts to a percentage by multiplying by 100. A fraction converts by the same step after it becomes a decimal, or by setting it over 100 directly. The denominator therefore decides the step.
A percentage greater than 100 means a fraction greater than one. One hundred and fifty per cent is therefore 150/100, which is larger than the whole it started from.
bullets: Per cent means over one hundred
Decimal to per cent: multiply by 100
Over 100 per cent means greater than one
content.takeaway: A percentage is a fraction over 100, so multiply by 100 to convert.

check.question: What is 0.35 as a percentage?

content.heading: Finding a percentage of a quantity
paragraphs: To find p per cent of a quantity, multiply the quantity by p and divide by 100. Fifteen per cent of 200 is therefore 15 × 200 ÷ 100 = 30. The division must follow the multiplication.
That method works for any quantity, whether it is money, mass or number. The quantity only changes the size of the product, not the method.
A percentage increase adds the percentage to the whole, while a percentage decrease subtracts it. A rise of 20 per cent on 50 is therefore 50 + 10 = 60, and a fall of 20 per cent is 50 − 10 = 40.
bullets: p per cent of Q is p × Q ÷ 100
Increase adds the percentage; decrease subtracts it
Method is the same for money, mass or number
content.takeaway: Multiply by p, divide by 100, then add or subtract for a change.

check.question: What is 20% of 150?

content.heading: Profit, loss and simple interest
paragraphs: Profit is selling price minus cost price, and loss is cost price minus selling price. A percentage profit is that profit over the cost price, multiplied by 100. The cost price is therefore the base.
Simple interest is I = P × R × T ÷ 100, where P is the principal, R is the rate and T is the time. The amount is then P + I. That formula needs the rate as a percentage, not as a decimal.
A trader who sells at a loss has a selling price below the cost price. That loss is therefore measured over the cost price as well, which is why profit and loss use the same base.
bullets: Profit = selling price − cost price, over cost price
Simple interest I = P × R × T ÷ 100
Amount = P + I
content.takeaway: Profit and interest are percentages over the cost price and the principal.

check.question: What is the simple interest on 500 at 6% per annum for 3 years?
check.why: 500 × 6 × 3 ÷ 100 = 90, so the interest is 90.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any percentage, name the base before computing. A profit base is the cost price, an interest base is the principal, and a change base is the original quantity. The wrong base gives the wrong answer.

steps.reason: Profit is 15 per cent of the cost price

steps.operation: Add the profit to the cost
steps.reason: Selling price is cost plus profit

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the base must be named
paragraphs: A percentage has no meaning without its base. Fifteen per cent of the cost price is not fifteen per cent of the selling price. That difference is why the base must be named before any computation.

Profit and loss therefore use the cost price because that is what the trader invested. A percentage profit that used the selling price would measure a different quantity. The base is therefore part of the definition.
Interest uses the principal for the same reason. The principal is what was borrowed, so the rate is charged on that amount. A rate on any other base would charge the wrong quantity.
That naming is the first step of every percentage question. A candidate who names the base cannot choose the wrong one.

content.heading: Go deeper: Increases, decreases and compound change
paragraphs: A percentage increase multiplies by one plus the rate, while a decrease multiplies by one minus the rate. A rise of 20 per cent on 50 is therefore 1.2 × 50. That multiplier is shorter than adding.
Two successive changes multiply. A rise of 10 per cent followed by a fall of 10 per cent is not the original, because 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99. That loss of one per cent is the product, not the sum.
A candidate who adds percentage changes therefore loses the mark. The changes must be multiplied as multipliers, which is why order matters.
That multiplication is why a fall after a rise does not restore the start. The base has changed, so the same percentage acts on a different quantity.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.objective: Use notation for sets and their operations to count elements in unions and intersections.

content.heading: Sets
paragraphs: A market in Jos lists yam buyers and rice buyers. A trader who buys both is counted in the overlap. That overlap is an intersection.

content.heading: What a set is and how it is written
paragraphs: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The elements of a set are its members, and a set is named by a capital letter. A set is written by listing its elements in braces.
An element that belongs to a set is written with the membership sign. If a is an element of A, it is written a ∈ A. If it is not, it is written a ∉ A. That sign is therefore the test of membership.
The empty set has no elements and is written ∅. A universal set U is the set of all objects under discussion. Every other set is therefore a subset of U.
bullets: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects
a ∈ A means a belongs to A; ∅ is the empty set
U is the universal set under discussion
content.takeaway: A set is defined by its elements, and membership is the test.

check.question: Which is the empty set?
check.why: The empty set has no elements, so it is written { } while {0} contains zero as an element.

content.heading: Union, intersection and complement
paragraphs: The union A ∪ B contains elements that are in A or in B or in both. It is the combined set without repetition. A yam buyer or a rice buyer therefore belongs to the union.
The intersection A ∩ B contains elements that are in both A and B. It is the overlap, and it is the smallest of the three operations. A trader who buys both therefore belongs to the intersection.
The complement A′ contains elements that are in U but not in A. It is therefore the set of non-members. That complement depends on U, which is why U must be named.
bullets: Union: in A or B; intersection: in both; complement: not in A
Union is combined without repetition
Complement depends on the universal set U
content.takeaway: Union combines, intersection overlaps and complement excludes.

check.question: A trader buys both yam and rice. In which set does she belong?
check.why: Both means in both sets, which is the intersection A ∩ B.

content.heading: Counting elements with Venn diagrams
paragraphs: A Venn diagram shows sets as circles inside a rectangle for U. The overlap of the circles is the intersection, and the rest of each circle is the exclusive part. The diagram therefore shows every region at once.
The number of elements in a union can be counted by addition with a correction. |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. The intersection is subtracted because it was counted twice.

A question that gives two sets and their union therefore needs the intersection, and a question that gives the sets and the intersection therefore needs the union. The formula works in both directions.
bullets: Venn diagrams show every region at once
Subtract the intersection because it was counted twice
content.takeaway: Add the two sets, then subtract the overlap counted twice.

check.question: If |A| = 10, |B| = 8 and |A ∪ B| = 15, what is |A ∩ B|?
check.why: 10 + 8 − 15 = 3, so the intersection has 3 elements.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any counting, name U and draw the Venn circles. A question that never names U has the whole class as U, and a complement that is counted without it will be wrong.

steps.reason: Add the sets, then subtract the overlap counted twice
Neither means in U but in neither set

hints: Find the union with |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|

content.heading: Go deeper: Subsets and the empty set
paragraphs: A is a subset of B when every element of A is in B. That relation is written A ⊆ B. The empty set is a subset of every set, because it has no element that could fail the test.
A set is equal to another when each is a subset of the other. That mutual inclusion is therefore the test of equality, not a comparison of size.
A proper subset excludes equality. It has fewer elements and every one is in the larger set. That exclusion is why ∅ is a proper subset of every non-empty set.
That definition is why the empty set is the most tested subset. It belongs everywhere without adding anything.

The empty set has no elements and is written as a pair of braces. That emptiness is why it is a subset of every set.

∅ is a subset of every set

content.heading: Go deeper: Venn diagrams with three sets
paragraphs: Three sets need three overlapping circles. Their overlaps create eight regions when the universal set is counted. Each region must be filled in turn, from the centre outward.
A question about exactly one set therefore names an exclusive region, while a question about at least one set names a union. That naming is the test of the region.
A question about neither set names the part of U outside all circles. That part is the complement of the union, which is why it is counted last.
That order is why a three-set question is solved from the centre. The overlaps are known first, and the exclusive regions follow from them.

lessons.title: Variation
lessons.objective: Use direct, inverse and partial variation to describe how one quantity changes with another.

content.heading: Variation
paragraphs: A trader pays four workers for six days and eight workers for three days. The product is the same. That constant product is inverse variation.

content.heading: Direct variation
paragraphs: Direct variation means y is proportional to x, written y = kx. The constant k is the ratio y ÷ x, which is the same for every pair. That sameness of the ratio is the test.
A quantity that varies directly with another therefore doubles when the other doubles. If y = 3x, then x = 2 gives y = 6 and x = 4 gives y = 12. The doubling is the meaning of k.
The graph of a direct variation is a straight line through the origin. That line is why a direct variation can be read from a single pair. One pair decides k for all.
bullets: Direct variation: y = kx, ratio y ÷ x constant
Doubling x doubles y
Graph is a straight line through the origin
content.takeaway: Direct variation keeps the ratio y ÷ x constant.

check.question: If y varies directly as x and y = 12 when x = 4, what is y when x = 7?

content.heading: Inverse variation
paragraphs: Inverse variation means y is inversely proportional to x, written y = k ÷ x. The product xy is therefore constant. That constant product is the test.
If x doubles, y halves. Eight workers for three days and four workers for six days are therefore the same total work. That halving is the meaning of the inverse relation.
The graph of an inverse variation is a hyperbola, not a line. A candidate who draws a line has therefore chosen the wrong variation.
That product can therefore be found from any single pair. Once it is known, any other pair can be worked out from it.
bullets: Inverse variation: y = k ÷ x, product xy constant
Doubling x halves y
Graph is a hyperbola, not a line
content.takeaway: Inverse variation keeps the product xy constant.

check.question: If y varies inversely as x and y = 6 when x = 5, what is y when x = 10?

content.heading: Partial variation
paragraphs: Partial variation combines a constant part with a varying part, written y = a + kx. The constant a is the value when x is zero. That intercept is the mark of a partial variation.
The varying part kx is direct. The whole therefore grows with x but starts from a. A taxi fare that has a flag-fall plus a distance charge is a partial variation.
The constant can be found from the graph where it crosses the y-axis. That crossing is the value at x = 0, which is why it is read first.
bullets: Partial variation: y = a + kx
a is the value when x is zero
The graph crosses the y-axis at a
content.takeaway: Partial variation is a constant plus a direct part.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the ratio and the product are constant
paragraphs: Direct variation means the quantities grow together. The ratio y ÷ x therefore cannot change, because a change in the ratio would break the proportional growth. That sameness is the definition.
Inverse variation means the quantities trade off. The product xy therefore cannot change, because an increase in one must be matched by a decrease in the other. That sameness is the definition.
A constant ratio and a constant product are therefore different tests for different variations. A candidate who uses the wrong one will get a wrong answer.
That distinction is why the variation must be named first. The name decides which quantity is constant.

In direct variation a change in x produces a proportional change in y, so the ratio between them is fixed. In inverse variation the product is fixed because a rise in one quantity must be exactly cancelled by a fall in the other to keep their product unchanged.

Name the variation before computing

content.heading: Go deeper: Graphs and what they show
paragraphs: A straight line through the origin is direct variation. Any other straight line is partial variation, because it has an intercept. That intercept is the constant part.
A hyperbola is inverse variation. Its shape comes from the product being constant, because as x grows large, y approaches zero without reaching it.
A graph that is neither a line nor a hyperbola is no simple variation. That shape therefore tells the candidate that another relation is at work.
That reading is why a graph can be questioned without numbers. The shape alone names the variation.
A hyperbola is inverse variation. Its shape comes from the product being constant, because as x grows large, y approaches zero without reaching it.

The straight line through the origin is the signature of direct variation. The curve that hugs both axes without ever touching either is the signature of inverse variation, because the product stays constant along every point of it.
bullets: Line through the origin: direct; line with intercept: partial
Hyperbola: inverse
Neither line nor hyperbola is no simple variation

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap in a variation question
paragraphs: The trap is a question that looks direct but is inverse, or the reverse. A candidate who does not name the variation will use the wrong constant. That naming is therefore the antidote.
The second trap is a partial variation that is read as direct. That error drops the constant part, which is why the intercept must be read first.
Time must be budgeted as in comprehension. A variation that resists can be left and returned to. A test that is finished is worth more than a perfect answer to three items.
That budget is why a first sweep is useful. The easy variations can be answered at once, and the hard ones can be left until the constant is clear.
The trap is a question that looks direct but is inverse, or the reverse. A candidate who does not name the variation will therefore use the wrong constant.

A candidate who names the variation first will choose the right constant and finish in under a minute. A candidate who starts computing first will often discover halfway that the wrong constant was used, which wastes the time the question was meant to save.
bullets: Name the variation before computing
A partial variation that is read as direct drops the constant
Do an easy-first sweep and return to hard items

lessons.title: Inequalities
lessons.objective: Use inequality signs to compare numbers, solve linear inequalities and represent solution sets on a number line.

content.heading: Inequalities
paragraphs: A shop in Lagos sells a bundle for more than 500 naira. The price is not a fixed number. That condition is an inequality.

content.heading: What an inequality means
paragraphs: An inequality compares two quantities that need not be equal. The signs <, >, ≤ and ≥ mean less than, greater than, less than or equal to and greater than or equal to. A solution is therefore a range, not a single number.
Flipping an inequality reverses its sign. If a < b, then −a > −b. That reversal happens whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, which is the trap most candidates miss.
Adding or subtracting the same number preserves the sign. If a < b, then a + c < b + c. Multiplying by a positive number also preserves it, while multiplying by a negative number reverses it.
bullets: Solutions to inequalities are ranges, not single numbers
Adding or subtracting preserves the sign
Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign
content.takeaway: An inequality states a range, and a negative multiplier reverses it.

check.question: If 3x < 12, which is true?
check.why: Dividing by the positive number 3 preserves the sign, so x < 4.

content.heading: Solving a linear inequality
paragraphs: A linear inequality is solved by the same steps as an equation, with one difference. Each step must preserve or correctly reverse the sign. A step that is valid for an equation can therefore be invalid for an inequality.

After isolating x, the solution must be checked against the original. A value that satisfies the final line but not the first step has been introduced by an illegal move. That check is therefore part of the method.
The solution is then represented on a number line. An open circle means the endpoint is excluded, while a filled circle means it is included. That distinction decides the sign.
bullets: Use the same steps as an equation, watching the sign
Check the solution against the original inequality
Open circle excludes; filled circle includes
content.takeaway: Solve like an equation, but reverse the sign for a negative multiplier.

check.question: If −2x ≥ 6, which is true?
check.why: Dividing by −2 reverses the sign, so x ≤ −3.

content.heading: Compound and fractional inequalities
paragraphs: A compound inequality gives two conditions at once, such as 2 < x ≤ 5. Its solution is the overlap of the two ranges. That overlap is therefore the answer, not either range alone.

A fractional inequality must have a common denominator before it is solved. The denominator can be negative, so its sign must be known before clearing it. That knowledge decides whether the sign reverses.
A quadratic inequality is solved by its critical values. The sign between them and outside them must be tested, because the expression changes sign at each critical value.
bullets: Compound: solution is the overlap
Fractional: know the sign of the denominator first
Quadratic: test the sign between and outside critical values
content.takeaway: Compound means overlap, fractional needs a known sign, quadratic needs a sign test.

check.question: What is the solution of 2 < x ≤ 5?
check.why: Both conditions must hold, so x must be greater than 2 and at most 5.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any dividing, ask whether the divisor is negative. If it is, the sign reverses; if it is positive, it does not. That one question decides most inequality traps.

content.problem: Solve −3x ≥ 9.

steps.reason: The divisor is negative, so the sign reverses

content.question: Solve 4x − 5 < 7. Keep the sign when dividing by 4.
hints: Add 5 to both sides first
Divide by the positive number 4
Represent the solution on a number line

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a negative multiplier reverses the sign
paragraphs: Multiplying by a negative reflects the number line. A number that was to the left of another moves to the right, so the order reverses. That reflection is why the sign must reverse.
Adding a constant shifts the line without reflecting it, so the order is preserved. That shift is why addition never reverses an inequality.
A candidate who understands the reflection will not need to memorise the rule. The rule is the geometry of the line.
That geometry is why the check matters. A solution that violates the original inequality has reflected incorrectly.
Multiplying by a negative reflects the number line. A number that was to the left of another moves to the right, so the order reverses.

Picture the number line being folded over. Every point that was to the left of the fold goes to the right of it, so a statement that was true before the fold is reversed after it. That folding is the geometry behind every sign reversal.
bullets: A negative multiplier reflects the line and reverses order
Addition shifts without reflecting
The check catches a wrong reflection

content.heading: Go deeper: Number lines and endpoint marks
paragraphs: An open circle means the endpoint is excluded. A strict inequality therefore has an open circle at its end. A filled circle means the endpoint is included.
A compound inequality has two endpoints, so it needs two marks. The overlap between them is shaded, which is why a compound line is a segment and not a ray.
A candidate who reads the marks has read the sign. The marks and the sign are therefore the same information in two forms.
That reading is why a number line can be questioned without words. The shaded part is the solution.
An open circle means the endpoint is excluded. A strict inequality therefore has an open circle at its end.

When a value is excluded, the boundary is not part of the solution and the circle stays open. When it is included, the boundary is part of the solution and the circle is filled. The mark therefore encodes the exact logical content of the sign.
bullets: Open circle excludes; filled circle includes
Compound solutions are segments between two marks
Marks and signs carry the same information

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap in an inequality question
paragraphs: The trap is a division by a negative that keeps the sign. A candidate who does not check the divisor will therefore write the reverse of the answer. That check is the antidote.
The second trap is a fractional inequality whose denominator is never signed. A candidate who clears it without knowing its sign will choose the wrong range.
Time must be budgeted as in comprehension. An inequality that resists can be left and returned to. A test that is finished is worth more than a perfect answer to three items.
That budget is why a first sweep is useful. The easy inequalities can be answered at once, and the hard ones can be left until the sign is clear.
The trap is a division by a negative that keeps the sign. A candidate who does not check the divisor will therefore write the reverse of the answer.

Reading the rule aloud before solving often prevents the error. Saying which sign will be used and why forces the divisor check to happen before any division is written, which is when it is too late to add.
That discipline is what separates the mark from the miss on the hardest inequality items.
bullets: Check the divisor sign before dividing
Know the denominator sign before clearing it
Do an easy-first sweep and return to hard items

lessons.title: Progression
lessons.objective: Find terms and sums of arithmetic and geometric progressions and solve problems that use progressions.

content.heading: Progression
paragraphs: A farmer adds the same number of bags to a pile each day. The pile grows by a constant addition each day. That constant addition is an arithmetic progression.

content.heading: Arithmetic progressions
paragraphs: An arithmetic progression adds the same number each term. That number is the common difference d, and the first term is a. The nth term is therefore a + (n − 1)d.
The sum of the first n terms is n/2 times twice the first plus (n − 1)d. That formula pairs the first and last terms, which is why it is half the number of terms times their sum.
A progression is therefore decided by two numbers. Once a and d are known, every term and every sum can be found. A candidate who knows those two knows the progression.
bullets: AP: constant difference d; nth term a + (n − 1)d
Sum is n/2 × (first + last)
Two numbers decide the whole progression
content.takeaway: An arithmetic progression is decided by its first term and its difference.

check.question: The first term of an AP is 3 and the difference is 4. What is the 5th term?

content.heading: Geometric progressions
paragraphs: A geometric progression multiplies by the same number each term. That number is the common ratio r, and the first term is a. The nth term is therefore ar^(n−1).
The sum of the first n terms is a(r^n − 1) ÷ (r − 1). That formula needs r not equal to one. If r equals one, every term is a and the sum is na.
A geometric progression grows by multiplication rather than addition. That growth is why a sum to a large n becomes large quickly, which is why the formula must be used.
bullets: GP: constant ratio r; nth term ar^(n−1)
Sum is a(r^n − 1) ÷ (r − 1) for r ≠ 1
r = 1 gives na
content.takeaway: A geometric progression is decided by its first term and its ratio.

check.question: The first term of a GP is 2 and the ratio is 3. What is the 4th term?

content.heading: Problems that use progressions
paragraphs: A word problem that gives a total and a number of terms needs the sum formula. A problem that gives two terms needs a and d or a and r. The given numbers therefore decide the formula.
A problem about a series of payments that grow by a constant amount is arithmetic, while a problem about growth by a constant factor is geometric. The story therefore names the progression.
A problem that asks for a term far down the list needs the nth term, not the sum. That distance is why the formula must be chosen before any numbers are used.
bullets: Total and number of terms need the sum formula
Constant addition is arithmetic; constant factor is geometric
A far term needs the nth term formula
content.takeaway: The story names the progression, and the givens choose the formula.

check.question: A farmer adds 2 more bags each day. Which progression is it?
check.why: A constant addition of 2 is an arithmetic difference.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before computing, name the progression and write its two numbers. For an arithmetic progression write a and d, for a geometric progression write a and r. The formula then follows without guessing.

content.problem: Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 3, 6, 9, …

steps.reason: Each term adds 3, so it is arithmetic with a = 3 and d = 3

content.question: Find the 6th term of 4, 12, 36, … . Name the progression first.
hints: Each term multiplies by 3, so it is geometric
Use ar^(n−1) with a = 4 and r = 3
Compute 3^5, then multiply by 4

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the formulas have their shapes
paragraphs: The sum of an arithmetic progression pairs the first and last terms. Each pair has the same sum, and there are n/2 pairs. That pairing is why the formula is half the number times their sum.

The sum of a geometric progression is found by subtracting the series from itself shifted by one term. The middle terms cancel, leaving a formula that depends only on the ends. That cancellation is why the formula is short.
A candidate who understands the pairing and the cancellation will not need to memorise. The formulas are therefore derivations, not magic.
That understanding is why a sum to a large n can be trusted. The pairing and the cancellation hold for every n.
The sum of an arithmetic progression pairs the first and last terms. Each pair has the same sum, and there are n/2 pairs.
Both derivations use the same idea: rewrite the sum so that most terms cancel. Pairing cancels the middle of an arithmetic sum, while shifting cancels the middle of a geometric sum.
bullets: AP sum pairs first and last terms
GP sum cancels middle terms by shifting
The formulas are derivations, not magic

content.heading: Go deeper: Infinite sums and the condition that decides them
paragraphs: An infinite geometric sum exists only when the ratio is between −1 and 1. If r is outside that range, the terms do not shrink and the sum grows without bound. That condition therefore decides whether a sum exists.
The limit is a/(1 − r) when the condition holds. That limit is the sum to infinity, not a sum to a large n. The two are therefore different quantities.
A problem that asks for a sum to infinity must first check the condition. A problem that asks for a sum to n needs no check.
That check is why an infinite sum is a separate topic. A candidate who skips it will write a number for a sum that has none.
An infinite geometric sum exists only when the ratio is between −1 and 1. If r is outside that range, the terms do not shrink and the sum grows without bound.
When the terms shrink, a large partial sum gets closer and closer to a single limit. When they do not shrink, each new term pushes the sum further away from any fixed value.
bullets: Infinite GP sum exists only for |r| < 1
Limit is a ÷ (1 − r)
Check the condition before writing the limit

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap in a progression question
paragraphs: The trap is an arithmetic progression that is read as geometric, or the reverse. A candidate who does not name the progression will therefore use the wrong formula. That naming is the antidote.
The second trap is a sum that is computed without checking whether the terms are those asked for. A sum to n is not a term, and a term is not a sum.
Time must be budgeted as in comprehension. A progression that resists can be left and returned to. A test that is finished is worth more than a perfect answer to three items.
That budget is why a first sweep is useful. The easy progressions can be answered at once, and the hard ones can be left until the numbers are clear.
The trap is an arithmetic progression that is read as geometric, or the reverse. A candidate who does not name the progression will therefore use the wrong formula.
Writing a and the constant beside the question before using any formula keeps the two numbers visible. Visible numbers are much harder to swap than numbers held in memory.
bullets: Name the progression before choosing a formula
A term is not a sum, and a sum is not a term
Do an easy-first sweep and return to hard items

lessons.title: Binary Operations
lessons.objective: Use the properties of a binary operation and find identity and inverse elements in simple cases.

content.heading: Binary operations
paragraphs: A trader in Kano tangles two numbers with a new rule, a * b = a + b + 1. Two numbers go in and one comes out, and the properties of that rule decide every mark here.

content.heading: What a binary operation is and closure
paragraphs: A customer buys 3 yam tubers at £4 each and 2 more, and the stall boy marks the new total with a star. The two counts combine into one total, and that combining is a binary operation.

A binary operation takes two elements of a set, in that order, and returns one element. It is called binary because two inputs are used. The operation * is not the multiplication sign here; it is only the name of the rule.

Closure means the answer never leaves the set. Whole numbers are closed under a * b = a + b + 1 because two whole numbers always give a whole number. Subtraction is not closed on whole numbers because 1 − 3 = −2 falls outside.
bullets: A binary operation combines two ordered elements into one element
Closure means the result stays inside the set
Subtraction fails closure: 1 − 3 = −2 leaves the set
content.takeaway: A binary operation needs two inputs and a result that stays in the set.

check.question: A binary operation * satisfies closure on a set when…
options: a * b is always in the set
a * b is never in the set
check.why: Closure only promises the result stays in the set; order and the addition formula are separate properties.

content.heading: Commutativity, associativity and distributivity
paragraphs: Two stall boys price two bundles in opposite order and get the same bill, so the customer asks whether order ever matters. Swapping the inputs is commutativity, and regrouping them is associativity, and the two are easy to confuse. Keep the test separate.

Test a * b = a + b + 1 on each property. Since 2 * 3 = 6 and 3 * 2 = 6, it is commutative, and since (2 * 3) * 4 = 11 and 2 * (3 * 4) = 11, it is associative. But 2 * (3 + 4) = 10 while 2 * 3 + 2 * 4 = 13, so it fails distributivity over addition.
bullets: Commutative: a * b = b * a for every pair
Associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) for every triple
Distributive over +: a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c
content.takeaway: Swap tests commutativity, regrouping tests associativity, brackets test distributivity.

check.question: For a * b = a + b + 1, which property holds?

content.heading: Identity and inverse elements
paragraphs: A stall keeper adds nothing to a pile and the pile stays the same, then removes what she added to return to the start. The do-nothing element is the identity, and the undoing element is the inverse.
An identity element e satisfies a * e = e * a = a. Here a + e + 1 = a gives e = −1. An inverse x satisfies a * x = x * a = e.
The inverse of 2 solves 2 + x + 1 = −1, so x = −4. Check: 2 * (−4) = 2 − 4 + 1 = −1, the identity. Identity leaves every element unchanged; inverse restores the identity.
bullets: a * e = e * a = a for every a
a * b = a + b + 1 has identity −1
Inverse of 2 is −4 since 2 * (−4) = −1
content.takeaway: Identity changes nothing, and an inverse undoes an element back to it.

check.question: Under a * b = a + b + 1, the identity element is
check.why: a * (−1) = a − 1 + 1 = a for every a.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Test closure first, then swapped inputs, then regrouped triples, then brackets expanded. Find the identity from a * e = a, and an inverse from a * x = e.

content.problem: For real numbers, a * b = a + b + 1. Find the identity element and the inverse of 3 under *.

steps.reason: The identity e must satisfy a * e = a for every a.
The e terms must cancel so the result is exactly a.
The inverse x must satisfy 3 * x = −1.

content.question: Find the inverse of 4 under a * b = a + b + 1.
hints: Write 4 * x = −1 using the identity −1
Simplify to 5 + x = −1
Solve for x and check that x * 4 is also −1

content.heading: Go deeper: Why distributivity matters when simplifying
paragraphs: Distributivity connects the new operation to the ordinary addition you already trust. That connection is what lets you expand a bracket such as a * (b + c) and compare it with a * b + a * c. Without it, the two operations would sit apart and every expression would need a fresh calculation.

Expansion is the daily use of distributivity. To simplify (a + b) * c you must spread * over the sum, just as multiplication spreads over addition in 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. The habit of spreading is the same even when the spread of a * b = a + b + 1 shows the spread failing.

Factoring is distributivity read backwards. Breaking a * b + a * c into a * (b + c) is exactly the step that gathers common terms. JAMB setters love the backwards step because it hides a simple form inside a longer one.

Conjugation is the same spirit applied to identities. Surrounding an element by an inverse and its undoing, x * a * x⁻¹, preserves the structure of a while moving the operation. You meet this idea when you solve a * x = e by multiplying through with the inverse.
The exam lesson is simple. Use distributivity when brackets must be opened, use it backwards when common terms must be gathered, and never spread an operation that has failed the test.
bullets: Distributivity bridges * and +: a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c
Expansion opens brackets; factoring gathers common terms
Conjugation x * a * x⁻¹ moves an element while preserving structure

content.heading: Go deeper: A harder case with a one-sided test
paragraphs: Some operations pass part of the test and fail the rest. Take a * b = a + 2b on the real numbers. Swapping gives 2 * 3 = 8 and 3 * 2 = 7, so it is not commutative.
Regrouping also fails: (2 * 3) * 4 = 8 * 4 = 16 while 2 * (3 * 4) = 2 * 11 = 24. The two groupings disagree, so associativity is out. Do not assume a property exists; test it with numbers first.

The identity test is subtler: setting a * e = a gives a + 2e = a, so e = 0. But the other side gives e * a = 2a, which is not a in general. A left identity that is not a right identity does not count as the identity.

Because the two-sided identity fails, no two-sided inverse can exist either. An inverse must tie to the identity, and there is none to tie to. That is why the exam always asks in the form does it exist, rather than expecting one blindly.
The safe habit is to test both sides of every identity claim. One side is never enough when the operation is not commutative.
bullets: a * b = a + 2b is neither commutative nor associative
e = 0 works only on the left, so no two-sided identity exists
No two-sided identity means no two-sided inverse

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap in a binary operation question
paragraphs: The commonest trap is habit. Candidates see * and assume multiplication, then carry over its commutativity and associativity. A defined operation is a new law, and the old laws must earn their place by testing.

The second trap is the reflexive identity. Candidates guess 0 or 1 because those are identities for addition and multiplication. Under a * b = a + b + 1 the identity is −1, and under a − b the right identity is 0 while the inverse of a is a itself.

The third trap is testing one pair and stopping. One matching pair never proves a property; all pairs must match. One failing pair, however, destroys it at once, which is why a single calculation can settle a question.

Time management beats brute force here. Test closure, then swap two numbers, then regroup three, then open one bracket. Each test takes seconds, and the pattern of passes and failures is usually written in the options.
Draw the tests in a short column before looking at the options. The column turns a guessing contest into a reading exercise, and reading exercises are won slowly and surely.
bullets: Never import multiplication habits into a defined operation
Find the identity by solving a * e = a, never by guessing 0 or 1
One failing pair destroys a property; one matching pair never proves it

lessons.title: Matrices and Determinants
lessons.objective: Perform matrix addition and multiplication, calculate 2x2 and 3x3 determinants, and find inverses of 2x2 matrices.

content.heading: Matrices and determinants
paragraphs: A shop records prices in columns and students record marks in rows. Matrices let us add, multiply and invert such tables. Determinants test whether a table can be inverted.

content.heading: What a matrix is and how to add matrices
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha records yam sales in the first row and rice sales in the second row. Each row lists Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday amounts. The whole table is a matrix, and each amount is an entry.
The order of a matrix is rows by columns. A table with two rows and three columns is order 2 by 3. The positions matter because rows and columns name different things.
To add or subtract two tables, the entries must line up. Corresponding entries are added or subtracted one by one. If the orders differ, the addition is impossible.
bullets: A matrix of order m by n has m rows and n columns
A matrix of order 2 by 3 has two rows and three columns
Matrices can be added only when they have the same order
content.takeaway: Same order allows addition entry by entry.

check.question: Which pair of matrices can be added?
check.why: Addition needs the same order so every entry has a partner.

content.heading: Multiplying matrices and why order matters
paragraphs: A caterer in Kano lists ingredient costs in one table and quantities in another. To find total cost she matches each cost with each quantity. That matching rule is matrix multiplication.
An m by n matrix multiplies an n by p matrix to give an m by p result. Each new entry adds products of a row with a column. If the inner numbers differ, the product cannot be formed.
Order changes the answer because the tables do different jobs. AB means apply B then A, while BA means apply A then B. These products are usually different and BA may not even exist.
bullets: An m by n times an n by p gives an m by p matrix
AB and BA are usually different because order changes the operation
BA exists only when the inner dimensions also match
content.takeaway: Check inner numbers and keep the order AB or BA.

check.question: Which statement about AB and BA is correct for most matrices?
options: AB and BA are usually different
AB is zero when BA is zero
AB is defined only when BA is undefined
check.why: Order matters, so swapping the factors usually changes the result.

content.heading: Determinants and the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix
paragraphs: Two traders pool money to buy goods. The owner writes two equations for the two prices. The determinant tells whether those equations give a unique answer.

For a 2 by 2 matrix with a, b on top and c, d below, the determinant is ad minus bc. For a 3 by 3 matrix, expand along any row and add signed 2 by 2 determinants. If the determinant is zero, the matrix has no inverse.

To invert a 2 by 2 matrix, swap the diagonal entries. Then negate the two off diagonal entries and divide every entry by the determinant. The result multiplied by the original gives the identity matrix.
bullets: A 2 by 2 determinant is ad minus bc
A 3 by 3 determinant expands with signed 2 by 2 determinants
The inverse swaps diagonal entries, negates off diagonal entries and divides by the determinant
content.takeaway: Compute ad minus bc, then swap, negate and divide.

check.question: What is the determinant of the matrix with rows 3 1 and 1 2?
check.why: Three times two minus one times one equals five.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Check orders first, then multiply in the order written. For a 2 by 2 inverse, compute ad minus bc before swapping anything. If the determinant is zero, stop because no inverse exists and tick the singular option.

content.problem: Find the inverse of the matrix with rows 3 1 and 1 2, that is A = [[3,1],[1,2]].

steps.reason: The inverse needs ad minus bc
Diagonal entries swap and off diagonal entries change sign
Every entry is divided by 5

content.question: Find the inverse of the matrix with rows 4 2 and 1 1.
hints: Compute the determinant with ad minus bc
Swap diagonal entries and negate off diagonal entries
Divide every entry by the determinant

content.heading: Go deeper: Identity, order and why AB and BA differ
paragraphs: The identity matrix I has ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. For any square A, multiplying by I leaves A unchanged on either side. That property makes I behave like the number one for matrices.

Think of a matrix as a set of instructions that moves points in the plane. A rotation matrix turns every point while a reflection matrix flips them. Doing the turn first and the flip second ends at a different point from the reverse order.

Geometry shows the gap for a point one space to the right of the origin. A quarter turn sends it up while a flip in the horizontal axis keeps it where it is. The two routes finish apart, so the products cannot be equal.

The identity also explains what an inverse must undo. A left inverse and a right inverse both return I, which is why the two-sided inverse is unique for square matrices. If no matrix returns I, the original has no inverse at all.

Zero behaves differently from identity. The zero matrix sends every point to the origin, so it destroys information. Adding the zero matrix changes nothing, while multiplying by it wipes the result out.
bullets: The identity I satisfies AI equals IA equals A
AB and BA differ because operations act in sequence
An inverse is a matrix that returns the identity
