On a number line the mean is the balance point of the data. Marks below the mean pull left and marks above pull right, and the pulls cancel. A mark far from the centre has a long arm, so it can balance a cluster near the centre.
bullets: Mean uses every value, so one outlier can pull it from mode and median.
A grouped mean is an estimate because each class uses its mark.
Total equals mean times count for finding a missing value.

content.heading: Go deeper: Quartiles and percentiles from the ogive
paragraphs: A percentile splits ordered data by percentage. The pth percentile has about p percent of values at most it. For twenty marks the 50th percentile is the median at cumulative frequency 10, the 25th is the lower quartile at cf 5 and the 75th is the upper quartile at cf 15, with each position given by p × n ÷ 100 (25 × 20 ÷ 100 = 5).

The ogive turns that definition into a reading by straight-line interpolation between plotted points. The lower quartile cf 5 lies between cf 3 at 9.5 and cf 10 at 19.5, giving about 13. The upper quartile cf 15 lies between cf 10 and cf 16, giving about 28, and the reading always goes across from the frequency axis, then down to marks.

The difference between upper and lower quartiles is the interquartile range, about 28 minus 13, which is about 15 marks. That range holds the middle half of the class and ignores both tails. Two classes can share median about 20 yet differ in spread, which is why quartiles add information the median alone cannot give.

The same reading also gives a proportion below any mark. Mark 19.5 has cumulative frequency 10, so 50 percent scored at most 19. Mark 29.5 has cf 16, so 80 percent scored at most 29, and either direction of the route gives the same answer when the axes are not swapped.
bullets: Lower quartile is the 25th percentile, median is the 50th, upper is the 75th.
Positions come from p × n ÷ 100 on the cumulative axis.
Interquartile range about 15 holds the middle half only.

content.heading: Go deeper: Drawing and reading a less-than ogive
paragraphs: A less-than ogive plots how many values are at most a boundary. The upper boundaries are 9.5, 19.5, 29.5, 39.5 with cumulative frequencies 3, 10, 16, 20, giving points (9.5, 3), (19.5, 10), (29.5, 16) and (39.5, 20). Join them smoothly from cumulative frequency zero, as plotting class marks on the horizontal axis is the common slip because the ogive answers at most a bound.

Cumulative frequency must rise and finish at the total 20. A final point other than 20 means a frequency was missed or repeated, while a falling curve means a frequency was subtracted. The curve should also steepen where frequencies are large, as around modal class 10–19 with frequency 7.

To find a value, move across from the required cumulative frequency to the curve, then down to the marks axis. To find a count below a mark, move up from the mark to the curve, then across to the frequency axis. A more-than ogive instead falls from 20 to zero, so the wording at most or more than decides which route to take.

Listing 3, 10, 16, 20 beside the upper boundaries before plotting prevents the most damaging error, which is plotting 3, 7, 6, 4. That single cumulative column carries the whole curve, and every percentile reading depends on it.
bullets: Plot cumulative frequency against upper boundaries, never class marks.
The curve must end at Σf = 20 and never fall.
At most uses the less-than route; more than reverses it.

lessons.title: Measures of Dispersion
lessons.objective: Compute range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and simple grouped data.

content.heading: Measures of Dispersion
paragraphs: Two classes average 10 marks, yet one class is steady and the other swings widely. The mean alone hides that difference, so dispersion measures how far scores spread around the mean.

content.heading: Range and mean deviation
paragraphs: Ada scores 7, 9, 10, 11, 13; Bello scores 6, 6, 10, 14, 14. Both classes average 10, but Ada clusters near 10 while Bello swings to 6 and 14. Something extra must describe that spread.
The range is the fastest look: highest minus lowest. For Ada range = 13 − 7 = 6; for Bello range = 14 − 6 = 8. A larger range warns extremes are far apart, though it uses only two scores.
Mean deviation uses every score. Find each distance from the mean, make it positive, then average: mean deviation = Σ|x − mean| ÷ n. For Ada: (3 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 3) ÷ 5 = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6.
bullets: Range = highest − lowest, so Ada's range is 6 and Bello's is 8.
Mean deviation = Σ|x − mean| ÷ n, so Ada's mean deviation is 1.6.
A larger range or mean deviation means scores spread farther from the mean.
content.takeaway: Range uses extremes only; mean deviation averages every distance.

check.question: For scores 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, what is the mean deviation about the mean?
check.why: Absolute deviations are 3, 1, 0, 1, 3, sum 8, and 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6.

content.heading: Variance and standard deviation
paragraphs: Ada's five deviations are −3, −1, 0, 1, 3, which add to zero. Averaging signed deviations therefore reports zero even though scores spread widely. Squaring fixes that cancellation.
Variance squares each deviation, averages the squares, and rewards large misses more. Variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n. For Ada: (9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 9) ÷ 5 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance: SD = √variance. It returns to the original units, so Ada's SD = √4 = 2 marks. Bello's variance is 12.8, so Bello's SD is about 3.58, clearly larger.
bullets: Variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n, so Ada's variance is 4.
Standard deviation = √variance, so Ada's standard deviation is 2.
Variance has squared units; standard deviation has the original units.
content.takeaway: Variance averages squared deviations; standard deviation returns to original units.

check.question: For scores 7, 9, 10, 11, 13 with mean 10, what is the variance?
check.why: Squared deviations sum to 20, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

content.heading: Grouped data and consistency
paragraphs: Instead of 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, a report groups them into classes 6–8, 9–11, 12–14. The exact scores vanish, so a class mark must stand for the whole class.
A class mark is the midpoint: (lower + upper) ÷ 2. The marks for 6–8, 9–11, 12–14 are 7, 10, 13, with frequencies 1, 3, 1. The grouped mean is Σfx ÷ Σf = (7 + 30 + 13) ÷ 5 = 10.

Now weight each squared distance by frequency: variance = Σf(x − mean)² ÷ Σf. Here (1×9 + 3×0 + 1×9) ÷ 5 = 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6, close to the exact 4. The smaller the variance or SD, the more consistent the data.
bullets: Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2 gives 7, 10, 13.
Grouped mean = Σfx ÷ Σf; variance = Σf(x − mean)² ÷ Σf.
The data set with smaller variance or standard deviation is more consistent.
content.takeaway: Use class marks as x, weight by f, and compare SD for consistency.

check.question: Classes 6–8, 9–11, 12–14 have marks 7, 10, 13 with frequencies 1, 3, 1. What is the grouped variance?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Write the mean first, then a deviation column, and divide by Σf for grouped data. Take the square root for SD; signed deviations must sum to zero as a quick check.

content.problem: Find the range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation for 7, 9, 10, 11, 13.

steps.reason: Add all scores and divide by 5, then subtract extremes for range.
Use |x − 10| for mean deviation and squares for variance.
Divide each sum by n = 5; root only for SD.

content.question: For scores 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, find the mean deviation and the standard deviation.
hints: Add the scores to get sum 50, then the mean 10.
List |x − 10| as 3, 1, 0, 1, 3 and average them for mean deviation.
Square the same deviations, sum to 20, divide by 5, then root for SD.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why squaring works and what the standard deviation means
paragraphs: Signed deviations always sum to zero, so their average is useless. For Ada: −3 −1 +0 +1 +3 = 0, exactly the same as five identical scores, yet the spread differs. Squaring removes signs without discarding size.

Squaring also punishes large misses more than small ones. A deviation of 3 contributes 9, while a deviation of 1 contributes only 1, so variance feels extremes strongly. Mean deviation treats them linearly, as 3 versus 1; that difference explains why variance and SD react more to outliers.

Variance lives in squared units, which cannot be compared with marks. Taking √variance returns the measure to marks, so SD = √4 = 2 marks for Ada. That return is why SD is quoted beside the mean and interpreted as a typical distance.

For Bello, squared deviations sum to 64, variance is 64 ÷ 5 = 12.8, and SD is about 3.58. The mean is the same 10, but SD 3.58 against Ada's 2 shows Bello's typical distance is larger. A quick check is the sum of deviations: it must be zero before you divide.

Exam questions often ask for both variance and SD from the same table. Compute Σ(x − mean)² once, divide for variance, then root for SD; never root before dividing. Mean deviation stays unrooted, which is why its 1.6 sits below SD 2 for this data.
bullets: Signed deviations sum to zero, so squaring is needed before averaging.
Variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n and SD = √variance keeps original units.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing between range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation
paragraphs: Range answers the quickest question: how far do extremes stretch? It needs only two scores, so it misleads when one outlier distorts the picture. Ada's range 6 versus Bello's 8 already hints at wider spread, but two scores cannot prove consistency.

Mean deviation uses every score but counts large and small moves linearly. That makes it calmer than variance when one score is extreme. For Ada the outlier 13 adds only 3 to the sum, so mean deviation stays 1.6 rather than exploding.

Variance and SD penalise extremes hardest because squaring magnifies them. A single far score can lift variance sharply, which is useful for risk questions but harsh for a single typo. In an exam, match the wording: 'average distance' suggests mean deviation, while 'square root of variance' names SD.

When the mean is near zero, comparing SDs across different scales misleads. The coefficient of variation, SD divided by the mean, puts spread on a relative scale. For two mark distributions both centred at 10, plain SD comparison is fair, which is why Bello's 3.58 beats Ada's 2.

JAMB ungrouped and simply grouped items use the mean and divide by n or Σf. That population form matches our totals: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 for grouped marks. If a question instead samples a population, it will state a different divisor, so read the stem before dividing.
bullets: Range uses extremes, mean deviation uses all scores linearly, SD uses squares.
Smaller SD means more consistent data when means are comparable.

content.heading: Go deeper: Grouped data, class marks and the shortcut formula
paragraphs: A class like 9–11 hides whether the true scores were 9, 10 or 11. The class mark 10 is therefore a representative, not a true value. Using it pretends every person scored 10, which explains why grouped variance slightly differs from the exact 4.

First find boundaries only if the question asks about them; JAMB usually asks through marks. Build columns for f, x, fx and f(x − mean)², with Σf = 5 and mean = Σfx ÷ Σf = 10. The f-weighted sum 18 then gives 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6.

The shortcut avoids subtracting the mean each row. Variance = Σfx² ÷ Σf − mean², because expanding (x − mean)² separates the terms. For our marks: 518 ÷ 5 − 100 = 103.6 − 100 = 3.6, exactly the row-by-row answer.

Check sizes before trusting the shortcut: Σfx² must exceed mean² × Σf, otherwise a sign error has crept in. Here 518 exceeds 500, leaving a small positive 18 after scaling, which is plausible because marks lie close to 10, while a negative result always signals a slip.

Interpretation stays the same: smaller grouped variance means the estimated scores cluster tighter. The grouped SD here is √3.6 ≈ 1.90, just below the exact 2, so the class-level story agrees even though the number is an estimate. Quote it as approximate when marks are involved.
bullets: Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2 represents every value in the class.
Grouped variance = Σf(x − mean)² ÷ Σf = Σfx² ÷ Σf − mean².

lessons.title: Permutation and Combination
lessons.objective: Solve simple problems involving permutations, combinations, linear and circular arrangements and repeated objects.

content.heading: Permutation and Combination
paragraphs: Market women in Lagos arrange five fabrics on a stall and choose three from eight for a display. Order matters in one task and not in the other. Permutation and combination count each situation correctly.

content.heading: Permutations: when order matters
paragraphs: Five books stand on Adebayo's shelf in Zaria. He wants to arrange three of them in a row for a photograph. The order of the three books is the point, so that is a permutation.

The factorial n! means multiply 1 up to n, so 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. To choose an ordered group of r from n, count n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the next, and so on down to n − r + 1.
That gives nPr = n!/(n − r)!. For the shelf, 5P3 = 5! / 2! = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 row arrangements. Positions such as first, second and third always signal a permutation.
bullets: A permutation is an ordered selection from n objects.
nPr = n!/(n − r)! counts ordered selections of r from n.
First, second and third positions mean order matters.
content.takeaway: Use nPr = n!/(n−r)! whenever the positions of the chosen objects matter.

check.question: Five books are arranged in a row. In how many ways can 3 be chosen and arranged?
check.why: 5P3 = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ordered arrangements.

content.heading: Combinations: when order does not matter
paragraphs: The school in Ibadan needs a class prefect team of three from ten volunteers. A team of Ngozi, Sule and Tobi is the same team as Tobi, Ngozi and Sule. Listing all six orders would count one team six times.
That situation is an unordered selection, called a combination. Start from the ordered count nPr and divide by the r! orders inside each group. So nCr = nPr ÷ r! = n! / (r!(n − r)!).

For the prefect team, 10C3 = 10! / (3! × 7!) = 10 × 9 × 8 ÷ 6 = 120. The cancellation leaves 10, 9 and 8, and dividing by 3! = 6 removes the six internal orders. A committee or a team drawn together asks for this count.
bullets: A combination is an unordered selection from n objects.
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) counts unordered selections of r from n.
The discrimination rule is simple: if swapping two members changes nothing, use combinations.
content.takeaway: Use nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!) when the order of the chosen objects does not matter.

check.question: A committee of 3 is chosen from 10 people. How many committees are possible?
check.why: 10C3 = 10 × 9 × 8 ÷ 6 = 120 unordered selections.

content.heading: Circular seats and repeated objects
paragraphs: Six friends sit round a circular table at a birthday in Enugu. A rotation of the whole table gives the same seating, because no seat is marked start. Fix one person and arrange the other five.
Fixing one person reduces a circle of n distinct people to (n − 1)! arrangements. For six people, 5! = 120 circular seatings. A straight row would have 6! = 720, which overcounts rotations.
Letters can repeat, so the plain factorial overcounts. The word MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with 4 I's, 4 S's and 2 P's. Divide 11! by 4! × 4! × 2! to remove the swaps inside each repeat.
bullets: Circular arrangements of n distinct people number (n − 1)!.
With repeats, divide n! by the factorials of each repeat count.
A stated head of the table or a starting seat restores n! arrangements.
content.takeaway: Circles use (n − 1)!; repeated objects end with division by repeat factorials.

check.question: Seven people sit round a table. In how many ways can they be seated?
check.why: (7 − 1)! = 6! = 720 circular arrangements.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In the hall, first ask whether order matters. Positions, ranks and row arrangements are permutations, while committees, teams and choice from a bag are combinations. Round a table, use (n − 1)!; with repeated letters, divide by each repeat factorial.

content.problem: A code uses 3 letters from the 8 letters A to H, with no letter repeated and order mattering. How many codes are possible?

steps.reason: Order matters and no letter repeats, so choose ordered positions.
First place 8 choices, then 7, then 6.

content.question: A team of 4 is chosen from 12 players for a relay. How many teams are possible?
hints: Order does not matter, so use nCr.
The count is 495 teams.

content.heading: Go deeper: How factorials build up and cancel
paragraphs: Counting choices place by place explains the factorial. Filling the first of four seats gives four choices, the next three, and so on down to one.
Multiplying those choices gives 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 for four distinct seats. Removing one seat leaves 3 × 2 × 1 = 6, which is why each missing place divides the count.
A permutation stops early when only r of n places are filled. Its product is n × (n − 1) × … × (n − r + 1), with r factors in all. Cancelling the untouched tail is exactly the step n! ÷ (n − r)!.

That view makes 7P3 = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210 immediate, without writing 7!. It also shows why nPr grows so fast when n and r grow together. One extra place multiplies the count by the number of choices left.
Exam calculation is therefore a cancellation exercise. Write n! over (n − r)!, cancel the shared tail, then multiply the short remaining product. No large factorial is ever needed.
bullets: Place-by-place choices multiply into n! and nPr.
nPr is n! with the untouched tail cancelled.
Cancel first, then multiply the short product.

content.heading: Go deeper: Symmetry and Pascal's triangle
paragraphs: Choosing r objects from n is the same as leaving n − r behind. The group chosen and the group left out are counted together, so nCr equals nC(n − r). That symmetry halves the work in an exam.
For example, 10C3 = 10C7. Computing 10 × 9 × 8 ÷ 6 = 120 is shorter than choosing seven. Always pick the smaller of r and n − r.

Pascal's triangle builds every combination by adding neighbours. Each entry equals the sum of the two entries above it, as in 10C3 = 9C2 + 9C3 = 36 + 84 = 120. The triangle therefore checks a binomial coefficient without factorials.
The edge cases are fixed by that construction. Choosing none or all gives one outcome, so nC0 = nCn = 1. Choosing one gives n, because each object forms its own singleton.

JAMB items often hide the symmetry. A question may ask for the ways to leave two pupils behind, which is the same count as choosing all others. Recognising the smaller group saves the factorial arithmetic.
bullets: nCr = nC(n − r): choosing and leaving match.
Each Pascal entry is the sum of its two neighbours.
nC0 = nCn = 1 and nC1 = n.

content.heading: Go deeper: Restrictions and repeated letters
paragraphs: A restriction fixes a place before counting the rest. If a particular book stands first on a shelf, arrange the remaining books freely in the other places. The fixed choice multiplies the free count by one.

Two people sitting together are glued into one block. A block of two plus n − 2 others gives (n − 1) objects, which are arranged in (n − 1)! ways round a line. The pair itself has 2! internal orders, so the total is 2 × (n − 1)!.

Repeated letters need the same idea: divide by the swaps that change nothing. The word MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with 4 I's, 4 S's and 2 P's. Its distinct arrangements number 11! / (4! × 4! × 2!) = 34650.

On a circle, repeats and rotations combine. Fix one distinct landmark, count the circle with (n − 1)!, then divide by the repeat factorials as in a line. Marking a head or a starting seat removes the rotation step.

The exam signal is the phrase that limits the count. Words such as first, together, identical and round a table each name one of these adjustments. Naming the adjustment before computing prevents the commonest overcount.
bullets: Fix a required place, then arrange the rest freely.
Two together: glue the pair, arrange, then order inside.
Distinct letters: divide by each repeat factorial.
